name: Spitzer
description: Four-player trick-taking game of the Schafkopf group (ace-ten family), played mainly in north-eastern Michigan, USA. Temporary partnerships each hand (two vs two or one vs three). Trumps are all queens, jacks, and diamonds; the diamond 7 (Spitzer) ranks second-highest. First to 42 game points wins.

content.text: Four-player trick-taking game of the Schafkopf group (ace-ten family), played mainly in north-eastern Michigan, USA. Temporary partnerships each hand (two vs two or one vs three). Trumps are all queens, jacks, and diamonds; the diamond 7 (Spitzer) ranks second-highest. First to 42 game points wins.

Spitzer is of the Schafkopf group of ace-ten games. It is played extensively in north-eastern Michigan (Rogers City, Alpena, Posen); regular tournaments are held. The game has clear German origins though definite evidence of play in Germany has not been found.

Four players. This is a trick-taking game; players form temporary partnerships each hand (two vs two or one vs three) but keep separate scores. The object is to be the first to reach 42 or more game points.
First dealer chosen by any method; deal passes left after each hand. Dealer shuffles, player to dealer's right cuts. Deal 8 cards to each player in packets: 3, then 2, then 3 to each.

items.text: Schneider in normal game: Some circles allow announcing Schneider in a normal partnership game; others do not.
Brush at 30 points: Some play that opponents need only 30 points for brush (not 31); then a Schneider announcement is to make at least 91 points.
